title: Constant-round MIS in the congested clique
formal: Is there a randomized algorithm that, on every n-vertex simple input graph, finds a maximal independent set in \(O(1)\) rounds in the Congested Clique model, with success probability at least $1-n^{-c}$ for every requested fixed $c>0$? Processor v initially knows its identifier and incident input edges. Every ordered pair of processors may exchange an \(O(\log  n)\)-bit message per synchronous round, whether or not the input edge exists. Each processor outputs whether it belongs to an independent set that dominates every vertex outside it. The algorithm must be uniform across inputs; it cannot be chosen after seeing the graph.
why: I include this beside the LOCAL MIS problem because it tests a different limitation of distributed computation: restricted bandwidth despite universal communication. A constant-round algorithm would show that exact local domination needs only a bounded number of global exchanges. A lower bound would have to explain why distributed processing cannot avoid the bottleneck.
definitions: Here $\Delta$ is the maximum degree of the input graph, not of the communication network. Messages to different recipients may differ. Local computation is unrestricted. $O(1)$ means independent of both $n$ and $\Delta$, with constants allowed to depend on the requested failure exponent. This is the unicast Congested Clique, rather than the weaker broadcast variant.

progress.text: Ghaffari, Gouleakis, Konrad, Mitrović, and Rubinfeld obtain the $O(\log\log\Delta)$-round MIS bound using sparsification.
Cambus, Kuhn, Pai, and Uitto obtain constant rounds for the 2-ruling-set relaxation.

Censor-Hillel, Even, Flin, and Halldórsson obtain constant rounds, for example, when average degree is at most $2^{O(\sqrt{\log n})}$. They also identify graph families on which existing sparsification methods require $\Omega(\log\log n)$ iterations. That restriction applies to those methods, not to all Congested Clique algorithms.

status_note: Reviewed 10 September 2026. Constant-round MIS on arbitrary input graphs remains open in the checked literature.

context_blocks.text: This changes the communication network while leaving the graph problem unchanged. A vertex can contact a distant processor immediately, so graph distance no longer limits the spread of information. Bandwidth still matters: one processor can receive only $O(n\log n)$ bits per round, whereas a general graph can contain $\Theta(n^2)$ independently specified edges. Sending the entire input to one leader is therefore not a constant-round solution.

That bottleneck is not itself a lower bound for MIS. A complete graph has many edges but is easy: a designated vertex can join the independent set and all others can stay out. The sought algorithm only needs enough information to coordinate a valid answer; it need not reconstruct every edge in one place.

Known algorithms exploit this by solving suitably sparse sampled subgraphs and reducing the remaining degrees. The general upper bound is $O(\log\log\Delta)$ rounds. The central question is whether a bounded number of communication phases can remove the need for repeated sparsification.

A closely related relaxation is already possible in constant rounds: a 2-ruling set remains independent but only has to put every vertex within distance two of a selected vertex. MIS requires distance one. This supplies a precise nearby success case against which to assess the unresolved target.

review_note: Individually written from the cited primary sources. The importance assessment is editorial. New preprint proofs have not been independently verified.
answer_criterion: Construct one randomized algorithm whose round bound is constant on every input graph, with the stated high-probability guarantee, or prove that constant rounds cannot suffice for all graphs in this model.

importance.reason: Asks whether all-to-all communication suffices for constant-round symmetry breaking, sharply testing the congested-clique model.

sentences: A maximal independent set is independent and places every excluded vertex next to a selected one.
In the congested clique, processors can send separate short messages directly to every other processor.
The question asks whether a randomized algorithm can solve this task in a constant number of rounds on every input graph with high probability.
Collecting all edges at one leader is too expensive, but the algorithm need not reconstruct the entire graph to choose a valid set.
The target is to replace repeated sparsification and degree-reduction phases with a bounded amount of globally coordinated communication.
